01.note: Of the twenty-four families of priests who took turns serving in the Temple, only four came back from the exile in Babylonia: Jedaiah, Harim, Pashhur and Immer. The prophets among the returnees divided these four into twenty-four new watches by drawing lots from a receptacle, each of the four families drawing its own lot and five more. The prophets also stipulated that if the family of Jehoiarib, which had originally headed the watches, ever returned, Jedaiah would keep first place and Jehoiarib would be subordinate to it.
01.why: The Gemara has been asking how Moses first set up the priestly watches, whether sixteen or eight, and how they grew to twenty-four; this teaching of the Sages carries the same question forward to how the twenty-four were rebuilt after the exile.

people.name: Jedaiah
people.about: One of the four priestly families that returned from exile; it was given first place among the watches.

people.name: Harim
people.about: One of the four priestly families that returned from exile.

people.name: Pashhur
people.about: One of the four priestly families that returned from exile.

people.name: Immer
people.about: One of the four priestly families that returned from exile.

people.name: Jehoiarib
people.about: The priestly family that originally headed the watches; it did not return, and would rank below Jedaiah if it did.

terms.meaning: The priests were divided into groups, each serving in the Temple for its own week in rotation.
The period after the First Temple was destroyed, when much of the Jewish people lived in Babylonia; some later returned to the Land of Israel.

02.note: A synagogue of the Jews of Rome opened onto a room where a corpse was lying, so the impurity of the dead spread into the synagogue, and the priests, who must avoid that impurity, could not go in to pray. They came to Rava, who told them to lift the ark and set it down in the opening between the rooms: a wooden utensil made to stay in one place cannot become impure, so it blocks the impurity. The Rabbis objected that the ark is sometimes moved with a Torah scroll still inside it, which makes it an ordinary movable utensil. Rava answered that if so, there is no remedy.
02.why: The Gemara is collecting Rava's rulings about the ark, its curtain and the cases that hold Torah scrolls; this case adds one more ruling of his about the ark, this time about its legal status as a wooden utensil.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage the priests consult; he proposes using the ark as a barrier, then concedes the objection.

terms.meaning: A dead body imparts the most severe form of ritual impurity, which spreads through a roofed space. Priests are forbidden to contract it.
The cabinet in a synagogue where the Torah scrolls are kept.

terms.term: a wooden utensil designated to rest
terms.meaning: In the purity laws, a large wooden object made to stay in place rather than be carried about cannot become impure, and so can act as a barrier against impurity.

03.note: Rav Huna once decreed a fast day. Rav Hana bar Hanilai and all the people of his town came to Rav Huna, and charity was imposed on them, which they gave. When they were about to go home, they asked Rav Huna to give the money back so they could support the poor of their own town with it. Rav Huna refused, citing a teaching that where a town has a scholar overseeing its needs, the money goes to him, and adding that the poor of his town and theirs alike rely on him.
03.why: A teaching just cited rules that townspeople who pledge charity while visiting another town take the money home for their own poor; this story shows the exception, when the town has a scholar in charge of its needs.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: The Sage who decreed the fast and kept the charity, saying the poor of both towns rely on him.

people.name: Rav Hana bar Hanilai
people.about: He came with the people of his town to Rav Huna on the fast day.

terms.meaning: A public fast declared by the community's leaders, often in time of trouble, when people also gave charity.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core text the Gemara discusses.
A Torah scholar responsible for managing a community's affairs, including the use of charity funds.

04.note: Rabbi Akiva asked Rabbi Nehunya the Great what virtue had earned him a long life. Rabbi Nehunya's attendants took the question as disrespect and began beating Rabbi Akiva, who climbed to the top of a date palm. From there he asked another question: if the Torah says the daily offering is a lamb, why does it add the word one? Hearing this, Rabbi Nehunya told his attendants that he was a young Torah scholar and to let him be. He answered that one means the finest of the flock, and that his long life came because he never accepted gifts, never insisted on getting even with those who wronged him, and was openhanded with his money.
04.why: The Gemara is explaining each of Rabbi Nehunya's virtues by pointing to the conduct of other Sages, and goes on to similar stories of Sages asked how they merited long life.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The young scholar who asks Rabbi Nehunya about his long life and is beaten by the attendants.

people.name: Rabbi Nehunya the Great
people.about: The aged Sage who stops his attendants and answers Rabbi Akiva.

terms.meaning: The lamb sacrificed in the Temple every morning and every afternoon.

05.note: Ravina and Rabba Tosefa'a were walking on the road when they saw a man drawing water with a bucket during the intermediate days of a Festival. Rabba Tosefa'a urged Ravina to excommunicate him. Ravina pointed to a teaching that one may draw for vegetables in order to eat them. Rabba Tosefa'a answered that the word there means pulling out crowded vegetables, not drawing water. Ravina then cited a teaching that says explicitly that one may draw water for vegetables, and Rabba Tosefa'a accepted it and withdrew his view.
05.why: The Gemara has just quoted a teaching that one may water vegetables during the Festival week in order to eat them but not to improve them; the story is an argument over what that teaching's word for drawing means.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: He defends the man drawing water, citing a teaching that permits it.

people.name: Rabba Tosefa'a
people.about: He wants the man excommunicated, then retracts when shown an explicit teaching.

terms.meaning: The days between the first and last days of Passover and Sukkot, when some work is permitted but heavy or unnecessary labor is not.
To place a person under a ban, cutting him off from the community, as a penalty for defying the Sages.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core text the Gemara discusses.

06.note: During the intermediate days of a Festival, the Bedita River overflowed and left large numbers of fish on its banks. Everyone went, caught fish and brought them home, and Rava permitted them to salt some of them. Abaye objected that one may preserve only food one can eat during the Festival. Rava replied that since they had brought the fish home intending to eat them, and the fish would spoil if left unsalted, they count as goods about to be lost, and salting them is permitted.
06.why: The mishna allows preserving only foods that can be eaten during the Festival week; this case tests that rule when far more fish arrived than could be eaten, and the discussion goes on to give a second version of Rava's ruling.

people.name: Rava
people.about: He permits the townspeople to salt the fish and defends the ruling.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: He challenges Rava's ruling from the mishna.

terms.meaning: The days between the first and last days of Passover and Sukkot, when some work is permitted but unnecessary labor is not.
The core early teaching of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses and explains.
A category of work allowed during the Festival week to prevent a financial loss that could not be avoided otherwise.

07.note: Two students, Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka and Rabbi Elazar ben Hisma, went to greet their teacher Rabbi Yehoshua in Peki'in. He asked what new idea had been taught that day in the study hall. They protested that as his students they could tell him nothing he did not know, but he insisted that a study hall is never without something new. They told him Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya had lectured on the mitzva of assembly: men come to learn, women to hear, and little children so that those who bring them are rewarded. Rabbi Yehoshua said they had held a fine pearl and tried to hide it from him. They then told him another teaching: God says to Israel, you have made Me one unique entity in the world, and I will make you one unique entity in the world.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka
people.about: A student of Rabbi Yehoshua who comes to greet him.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Hisma
people.about: A student of Rabbi Yehoshua who comes to greet him.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Their teacher, who presses them for the day's new teaching.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: The Sage who gave that week's lecture in the study hall.

terms.meaning: The Torah's command that the whole people, men, women and children, gather once every seven years to hear the Torah read.
The house of learning where the Sages taught and debated Torah.

08.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi made a wedding for his son, Rabbi Shimon. On the wedding canopy was written that 24,000 myriad dinars had been spent on it, yet he did not invite bar Kappara. Bar Kappara said: if those who go against God's will get such reward, how much more those who do His will. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi then invited him, and bar Kappara said: if those who do His will get this much in this world, how much more in the World-to-Come. In another episode, because calamity struck the world on any day Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi laughed, he offered bar Kappara forty se'a of wheat not to make him laugh. Bar Kappara put a tar-smeared basket upside down on his head and came to collect his wheat; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi laughed, and bar Kappara said he was only taking what he was owed.
08.why: The discussion has moved from kinds of figs to a story of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi marveling at a thousand fig dishes; it continues with stories of his wealth and his dealings with bar Kappara.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: The wealthy leader who makes the wedding and who tries to keep bar Kappara from making him laugh.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: The son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, whose wedding this is.

people.name: bar Kappara
people.about: A Sage left off the wedding guest list, known here for his sharp wit.

terms.meaning: Ten thousand.
A silver coin; the sum on the canopy is meant to sound enormous.
A measure of volume for grain.
The reward of the righteous after this life.

09.note: Isi bar Yehuda stayed away from Rabbi Yosei's academy for three days. Vardimus, Rabbi Yosei's son, found him and asked why. Isi said he could not attend when he did not understand Rabbi Yosei's reasoning, and named the puzzle: Rabbi Yosei teaches that a town's own laundry takes precedence over the lives of others, but what verse is that based on? Vardimus explained it from the verse about the land around the Levite cities, which is for their animals and for all their beasts. The word for beasts can also be read as their lives, and since that would be obvious, it must mean something vital to life, namely laundry, because grimy clothes cause real suffering.
09.why: The Gemara returns to Rabbi Yosei's ruling that a town's laundry comes before others' lives, and the story supplies the verse behind it before the discussion turns to Rabbi Yosei's view of vows about bathing.

people.name: Isi bar Yehuda
people.about: A student who stopped attending Rabbi Yosei's academy because he could not follow one of his rulings.

people.name: Vardimus
people.about: The son of Rabbi Yosei, who explains his father's reasoning.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage whose academy Isi attended and whose ruling puzzled him.

terms.meaning: A house of Torah study headed by a Sage.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core text the Gemara discusses.
Towns the Torah assigned to the tribe of Levi, with open land around them.

10.note: Rabbi Meir recalled that while studying with Rabbi Akiva he used to add iron sulfate to the ink he wrote Torah scrolls with, and Rabbi Akiva said nothing. When he came to study with Rabbi Yishmael, Rabbi Yishmael asked his trade, and on hearing he was a scribe warned him to be careful, since leaving out or adding a single letter could destroy the whole world. Rabbi Meir replied that he put iron sulfate into his ink. Rabbi Yishmael objected: the Torah says the curses of the sota scroll are to be blotted out, so the writing must be erasable.
10.why: The mishna has just described the woman suspected of adultery drinking the water into which the scroll's curses are blotted; the Gemara opens with this exchange over ink that cannot be erased, then raises a version with the teachers reversed.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: A scribe of Torah scrolls who tells of studying with two teachers.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: One of Rabbi Meir's teachers, who did not object to his ink.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: Another teacher of Rabbi Meir, who warned him about his work and his ink.

terms.meaning: A substance added to ink to make the writing permanent so it cannot be washed off.
A wife suspected of adultery. In the Temple rite, curses were written on a scroll and dissolved in water that she drank.
One who writes Torah scrolls and other sacred texts by hand, where every letter must be exact.

11.note: Yohanan the High Priest sent messengers throughout the Land of Israel and found that people set aside only the main priestly gift from their produce, while some gave the first and second tithes and some did not. He told them that eating produce without the tithe of the tithe taken, or untithed produce, carries a penalty of death at the hand of Heaven, just as with the main gift. He then made an ordinance: anyone who buys produce from an unlearned person must set aside the first and second tithes himself. The tithe of the tithe goes to a priest and the second tithe is eaten in Jerusalem, but the Levite and the poor cannot demand their shares without proof.
11.why: The mishna says Yohanan the High Priest abolished the declaration of tithes; the Gemara had explained that people gave the tithe to priests rather than Levites, and this account, showing many did not tithe at all, challenges that, leading to the answer that he made two separate ordinances.

people.name: Yohanan the High Priest
people.about: He investigated tithing across the land and instituted the ordinance on doubtfully tithed produce.

terms.meaning: The main gift from a harvest that must be given to a priest before the produce may be eaten.
Tenths of produce: the first tithe goes to the Levites, who give a tenth of it to priests; the second tithe is eaten by its owner in Jerusalem; the poor man's tithe goes to the poor.
An unlearned person, who could not be trusted to have set aside the required tithes.
Produce bought from someone who may not have tithed it; Yohanan's decree requires the buyer to tithe it.

12.note: The Roman government once sent two military officials to the Sages of Israel with an order: teach us your Torah. They read it through three times. As they left, they said they had examined the whole Torah and found it true, except for one rule: if a Jew's ox gores a gentile's ox the owner is exempt, but if a gentile's ox gores a Jew's ox he pays in full. Either the Torah's words of another apply only to Jews, and then the gentile should be exempt too, or they apply to everyone, and then the Jew should pay too. But they said they would not report this to the government.
12.why: The Sages tell this story in connection with the rule the officials challenge, the different treatment of a Jew's ox and a gentile's ox, which the Gemara has just been discussing.

terms.meaning: An innocuous ox has no record of goring and its owner pays half the damage; a forewarned ox has gored before and its owner pays in full.
Words from the Torah's law of goring oxen, about an ox that gores the ox of another person.

13.note: The daughter of Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda died. The Sages asked Ulla to come with them to console him, but he refused: the Babylonians console mourners by saying what can be done, which implies they would act against God's decree if they could, and he called that heresy. He went alone and spoke to the father about God telling Moses not to make war on Moab. Moses had reasoned that if the Torah ordered Israel to strike the Midianites, who only helped Moab, then surely Moab itself should be attacked. God answered that He had two good fledglings to bring out of them, Ruth the Moabite and Naamah the Ammonite. Ulla reasoned that if God spared two great nations for two such women, then if the daughter had been righteous and fit to bring good into the world, she would surely have lived.
13.why: The story is told in passing after the account of the Roman officials, and its mention of Moab and Ammon leads the Gemara on to a teaching that God rewards even refined speech.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda
people.about: A Sage whose daughter died; Ulla calls him his teacher.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: He refuses the Babylonian form of consolation and goes alone to comfort the father.

people.name: Moses
people.about: In Ulla's words, he reasoned that Moab should be attacked and God stopped him.

people.name: Ruth the Moabite
people.about: Named by God as one of the two good fledglings for whose sake Moab was spared.

people.name: Naamah the Ammonite
people.about: Named by God as the other good fledgling, for whose sake Ammon was spared.

terms.meaning: An argument from a lesser case to a greater one: if this is true here, it is all the more true there.
Neighboring peoples who, in the Torah, joined against Israel in the wilderness.

14.note: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel applied the verse "My eye affected my soul, because of all the daughters of my city" to his own family: there were a thousand children in his father's household, five hundred studying Torah and five hundred studying Greek wisdom, and the only ones left were himself and his cousin in Asia Minor. The Sages explained that Rabban Gamliel's household was different because it was close to the government, just as they allowed Avtolmos bar Reuven, who was also close to the government, to cut his hair in the Roman style.
14.why: The Gemara has cited a curse on anyone who teaches his son Greek wisdom; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's account seems to show it was studied freely in his father's house, and the Sages explain why that family was an exception.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: He tells of the thousand children in his father's household, of whom only he and a cousin remained.

people.name: Avtolmos bar Reuven
people.about: A man close to the government who was allowed to wear the Roman-style haircut.

terms.meaning: Greek learning and culture, which the Sages restricted at a time of war with Rome.
A Roman hairstyle; adopting it was treated as following the ways of the gentiles.
Gentile customs that the Torah forbids Jews to imitate.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core text the Gemara discusses.

15.note: Rabbi Yirmeya's brother-in-law, a minor, shut the doors of his late father's house against Rabbi Yirmeya, who claimed part of it. Rabbi Yirmeya took the case to Rabbi Avin, who said the boy was holding what was his. Rabbi Yirmeya offered witnesses that he had taken possession while the father was alive, but Rabbi Avin said testimony is not accepted in the absence of the other party, and a minor cannot stand as one. Rabbi Yirmeya protested: had the whole world lined up behind Sumakhos to take away what was his? The case reached Rabbi Abbahu, who cited a ruling that land a child seizes is taken from him at once, and he may bring witnesses when he grows up. The Gemara rejects that comparison, since this boy inherited the house; the text does not say how the case ended.
15.why: The Gemara has just cited a teaching on whether minor heirs must return what their father stole, with Sumakhos disagreeing; this case turns on that dispute and leads into a discussion of testimony given when a party is absent.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: He claims a share of his father-in-law's house and is shut out by his young brother-in-law.

people.name: Rabbi Avin
people.about: The judge who first hears the case and favors the boy.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: The Sage the case finally reaches; he cites a ruling in Rabbi Yirmeya's favor.

people.name: Sumakhos
people.about: An early Sage who held that minor heirs are exempt; Rabbi Avin points to his view.

terms.meaning: A child under the age of legal adulthood, who cannot be a party to a court case.
A legal assumption that whoever holds property, here by inheriting it, owns it unless proven otherwise.

16.note: A man from Naresh stole a scroll and sold it to a man from Pappunya for eighty dinars, who sold it on to a man from Mehoza for one hundred and twenty. Then the thief was identified. Abaye ruled that the owner should pay the man from Mehoza eighty dinars and take back his scroll, and the man from Mehoza should collect the other forty from the man from Pappunya. Rava objected and ruled instead that the owner pays the full one hundred and twenty, then collects forty from the man from Pappunya and eighty from the thief from Naresh.
16.why: The Gemara is working through cases of the Sages' ordinance that an owner pays to reclaim stolen goods from an innocent buyer; this case asks how it applies when the item passes through a second buyer.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: He gives the first ruling on how the payments should be divided.

people.name: Rava
people.about: He objects to Abaye and gives a different division.

terms.meaning: An ordinance of the Sages: an owner who reclaims stolen goods from an innocent buyer repays the buyer's price, so that people are not afraid to buy in the market.
A silver coin.

17.note: A man left money in another's care. The guardian gave it to his mother, who put it in a chest, and it was stolen. Rava asked how judges should rule. The guardian cannot simply be ordered to pay, because anyone who leaves something in another's care knows that his family may look after it. The mother cannot be ordered to pay, because her son never told her the money was not his, or she would have buried it. And the son can say that letting her think it was his made her even more careful. Rava ruled that the son swears he gave it to his mother, she swears she put it in the chest and it was stolen, and the son is exempt.
17.why: The Gemara is gathering rulings on when a guardian of money is negligent, such as hiding it in a willow hut or forgetting where it is; this case asks whether handing it to a family member counts.

people.name: Rava
people.about: He works through each party's defense and rules on the case.

terms.meaning: Someone who agrees to look after another person's property and may have to pay if it is lost through negligence.
A solemn sworn statement in court, used to settle claims that cannot otherwise be proven.

17.flag: The STORY segments stop before Rava's ruling (oaths, guardian exempt), which falls in AFTER segment 9; the boundary probably should include it.

18.note: A guardian handling the affairs of orphans bought them an ox and handed it to a cowherd. The ox had no molars or teeth to eat with, and it died. Rami bar Hama asked how judges should rule. The guardian can say he gave it to the cowherd, and the cowherd can say he put it with the other oxen and threw it food, not knowing it did not eat. Since the orphans got their money back from the seller, the Gemara reasons, the claim comes from the seller, a trader who did not know of the defect: he swears he did not know, and the cowherd pays him the value of the meat at the cheapest price.
18.why: The Gemara is working through a run of cases in which property in someone's care passes through several hands and is lost, each asking how judges should rule; this one follows Rava's case of the guardian who gave money to his mother.

people.name: Rami bar Hama
people.about: The Sage who poses the question of how judges should rule.

terms.meaning: Someone paid to look after another's property; he must pay for losses caused by his lack of care.
A sale of an item with a hidden defect, which can be undone so the buyer gets his money back.
A person appointed to manage the property of orphans who are too young to manage it themselves.

19.note: A man left hops, used in making beer, in another's care. The guardian also had his own pile of hops, and he told his brewer to use hops from this pile, but the brewer went and used the other pile, the one left in his care. Rav Amram asked how judges should rule. The guardian can say he told the brewer which pile to use, and the brewer can say he was never told not to use the other one. The story itself does not give a ruling.
19.why: One of a run of cases in which property left in someone's care is lost through another person's hands; the discussion that follows asks whether the guardian is still to blame and what loss there really was.

people.name: Rav Amram
people.about: The Sage who poses the question of how judges should rule.

terms.meaning: A plant used in brewing beer.
Someone who agrees to look after another person's property and may have to pay if it is lost.

20.note: Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis disputed whether a certain oven could become impure. Losing the argument, he called on a carob tree, a stream and the study hall walls to prove him right; each did, and the Rabbis rejected each. A Divine Voice declared that the law follows him, yet Rabbi Yehoshua answered, "It is not in heaven." Elijah later told Rabbi Natan that God smiled and said, "My children have triumphed over Me." The Sages burned what Rabbi Eliezer had declared pure and ostracized him. Rabbi Akiva, dressed in black, told him. He wept, crops were struck, and what he looked at burned. Rabban Gamliel nearly drowned until he prayed. Later his wife Imma Shalom, Rabban Gamliel's sister, found him praying face down and said, "You killed my brother"; just then a shofar announced his death.
20.why: The Gemara brings the story apropos of verbal mistreatment: it ends with Imma Shalom's teaching that the gates of prayer stay open for those who are wronged by words, and the discussion goes on to the verbal mistreatment of converts.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage who stands alone against the Rabbis on the oven and is ostracized.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: He rebukes the walls and rejects the Divine Voice, saying the Torah is not in heaven.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's disciple, who volunteers to tell him of his ostracism.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The head of the Sages who ostracized Rabbi Eliezer; Imma Shalom's brother.

people.name: Imma Shalom
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's wife and Rabban Gamliel's sister, who guards her husband's prayers.

terms.meaning: A voice from Heaven that announces God's view; here the Sages refuse to decide law by it.
Placed under a ban: others must keep their distance, and the person behaves like a mourner.
The posture of a personal supplication prayer said after the main prayer; it is skipped on the New Moon.
A ram's horn; here it is sounded to announce a death.
